# MOOD

## An Open Coordination Protocol and Digital World for Human and Machine Agency

**Identity · Contribution · Proof · Reputation · Agents · Nodes · Governance · Settlement**

> **MOOD is the world. Moodify is only the beginning.**

Version 0.1 · August 2026 · crestwavecoin.com

Technical architecture and protocol design paper. This document does not constitute investment advice, a promise of returns, or an offer of securities.


## Machine-Readable Canon Notes

This Markdown file is the Codex-oriented text edition of the MOOD English Whitepaper v0.1.

When using this document for implementation, preserve the following hierarchy and boundaries:

- **MOOD** is the open digital world and coordination network.
- **WORLD**, **PROTOCOL**, and **PORTAL** are the three top-level interface layers bound to shared network state.
- **Moodify Protocol** is the genesis vertical for sound, AI, evidence, verification, and domain-specific outputs.
- **Moodify** is the genesis application and first real workload; it is not the boundary of MOOD.
- **MOOD Token** is the native economic coordination asset and value layer; it is not identical to MOOD the world.
- Root MOOD primitives should remain domain-general. Sound-specific semantics belong in Moodify Protocol.
- Design targets in this paper are not automatically deployed facts. Contract addresses, issuance parameters, node counts, governance powers, and other live-state claims must be checked against the canonical implementation and network interface.
- Prefer modular protocol components and explicit versioning over a monolithic architecture.
- Existing smart-contract networks may be used for settlement and commitments; an independent MOOD L1 is not a prerequisite.

# Abstract

The internet has become exceptionally good at distributing software, media, capital and information, yet most digital collaboration still depends on platform-owned identities, opaque contribution histories, centralized permissions and organization-specific databases. At the same time, artificial intelligence is becoming an active participant in production: agents can write code, analyze media, perform research, operate tools and coordinate workflows, but there is no general open network in which human and machine actors can acquire durable identity, accept tasks, produce verifiable evidence, accumulate reputation, access resources, participate in governance and settle value under shared public rules.

MOOD proposes an open digital world and protocol network for this coordination problem. It is not a single application, a token wrapper, or a claim that every interaction should be placed on a blockchain. MOOD separates the human-facing world, the public rule system and the participation interface into three layers - WORLD, PROTOCOL and PORTAL - while binding them to a shared network state. The state is composed of identities, agents, nodes, tasks, contributions, proofs, reputation, rights, governance decisions and economic commitments. A valid network action is a state transition whose authorization, evidence and verification requirements are defined by versioned protocol modules.

The first practical workload is Moodify, a sound-and-AI protocol and genesis application. Moodify exists to prove the general primitives with real work: tasks, model or human execution, evidence, verification, contribution records, reputation and settlement. Sound is therefore the genesis of MOOD, not the boundary of MOOD. Future protocols and applications may coordinate research, compute, creative production, software development, curation, public goods and other forms of human-machine cooperation.

This paper specifies the conceptual state model, participant types, proof lifecycle, agent and node semantics, economic layer, governance process, hybrid on-chain/off-chain architecture, security assumptions, scalability strategy and genesis roadmap. MOOD is designed protocol-first and chain-agnostic. Early versions may use existing smart-contract networks for settlement and cryptographic commitments while keeping large artifacts and rich execution state off-chain. The purpose is not to maximize financialization. The purpose is to make digital cooperation enterable, inspectable, participatory and verifiable.

## Core proposition

> Bitcoin made decentralized monetary state credible. Ethereum generalized programmable state. MOOD explores a different abstraction: open coordination state for humans, AI agents and network resources.

## Status of this paper

This document is a design specification and architectural thesis. It distinguishes protocol targets from deployed facts. Any contract address, issuance parameter, network count, node status or governance power must be verified against the live canonical interface and versioned implementation before being treated as operational truth.

# 1. Motivation and Historical Context

## From platform ownership to protocol coordination

The dominant architecture of the consumer internet is the platform. A platform offers useful software but also owns the account system, internal reputation, ranking logic, permissions, moderation rules, application programming interfaces and most of the historical record that gives a participant standing inside that environment. A creator can accumulate years of work and audience on one platform while remaining almost unknown to another. A developer can contribute to several communities while their history is fragmented across repositories and databases. A company can coordinate employees and vendors because it controls identity, payroll and access, but the coordination mechanism normally ends at the boundary of the company.

Blockchains introduced a different organizational primitive: publicly inspectable state governed by rules that no single application interface has to own. Bitcoin showed that a network can agree on a monetary history without a central issuer. Ethereum generalized the idea by allowing developers to define arbitrary state transition logic in smart contracts. The larger implication is not that every system should become a blockchain. It is that public state, cryptographic authorization and shared rule execution can make forms of coordination possible outside the boundary of a single firm or platform.

## The arrival of machine participants

Artificial intelligence changes the coordination problem again. Software agents are no longer limited to deterministic background jobs. Modern agents can interpret goals, call tools, write code, analyze media, summarize evidence, propose actions and maintain long-running workflows. A future network will therefore coordinate not only people and servers but also semi-autonomous actors whose outputs must be attributed, constrained, evaluated and, in some cases, paid for. Existing account systems were not designed for this. A wallet can sign a message, but it does not explain whether the signer is a person, an agent, a node, a delegated service or a multisignature organization. A transaction can transfer value, but it does not by itself prove that useful work occurred.

MOOD begins from this gap. The question is not merely how to pay an AI agent. The question is how a heterogeneous population of people, agents, models, applications and resource providers can participate in a persistent open network under rules that make actions inspectable and histories durable. The network needs identity without reducing identity to wealth, contribution records without confusing activity with quality, reputation without a single centralized scorekeeper, and settlement without pretending that every form of value is financial.

## Why a digital world, not only a protocol

A protocol can be technically correct and socially empty. People do not inhabit data structures; they inhabit places, cultures, narratives and interfaces. MOOD therefore uses the term digital world deliberately. WORLD is the human and cultural surface through which participants understand where they are and why they may wish to remain. PROTOCOL is the public rule layer that makes the world more than a brand. PORTAL is the action layer through which a visitor becomes a resident, contributor, agent owner, node operator or governor. All three are required to create a network that is simultaneously meaningful and inspectable.

```text
MOOD
├── WORLD      meaning / culture / place
├── PROTOCOL   rules / proof / governance
└── PORTAL     identity / action / history
        │
        ▼
SHARED NETWORK STATE
people · agents · nodes · tasks · contributions · reputation · rights · settlement
```

**Figure 1.** The three interface layers converge on one shared network state.

# 2. Design Objectives and Non-Goals

## Objectives

- Open participation: people, agents, developers, creators, researchers and resource providers can enter without requiring employment by a single operating company.

- Verifiable history: important contribution, governance and settlement actions can be traced to evidence and protocol versions.

- Modular trust: different domains may use different verification methods instead of forcing one universal notion of truth.

- Portable identity: a Passport represents durable network history while remaining separable from any single wallet address.

- Human-machine parity where appropriate: agents can become first-class actors for task execution, but high-risk authority can remain explicitly delegated and revocable.

- Real contribution before reward: economic incentives follow work, service, verification or explicit governance rules rather than presentation-only activity.

- Progressive decentralization: early systems may retain necessary administrative controls, but powers, keys and upgrade paths must be documented and reducible over time.

- Chain pragmatism: existing smart-contract networks may provide settlement and commitments; MOOD does not require an independent chain to prove its thesis.

## Non-goals

MOOD is not a universal truth machine. It does not assume that subjective judgments can be converted into objective consensus. It is not a promise to place all user data on-chain. It is not a mechanism in which holding more tokens automatically makes an identity more reputable. It is not a node-sale economy in which purchasing a license is treated as productive service. It is not an autonomous treasury controlled by an opaque AI. It is not a replacement for every application. Applications remain important; the protocol exists so that applications can share identity, proofs and coordination primitives without owning the entire network relationship.

MOOD also does not assume that decentralization is binary. A network can have public state and open contribution while using centralized services for convenience; it can have decentralized settlement while retaining human security keys during an early stage. The relevant requirement is legibility: users should be able to distinguish which claims are cryptographically enforced, which are socially governed, which depend on a service operator and which are merely planned.

# 3. System Overview

## Canonical architecture

The canonical interface architecture is MOOD = WORLD + PROTOCOL + PORTAL. WORLD provides culture, spatial metaphor, public memory and orientation. PROTOCOL defines the rules governing identity, proof, agents, nodes, governance, economics and security. PORTAL exposes the actions by which a participant connects a wallet, creates or links a Passport, contributes work, registers agents or nodes, receives rights and participates in governance. The three surfaces should not maintain contradictory states; they are views over one shared network.

## Shared network state

At a conceptual level, the network state is not only a ledger of token balances. It is a graph of actors and claims. It includes identities and their keys, delegated agents, registered nodes, active tasks, submitted artifacts, evidence commitments, verification outcomes, contribution records, reputation values, permissions, governance proposals, treasury commitments and settlement events. Some of this state is naturally public and compact; other state is large, private, ephemeral or domain-specific and should remain off-chain while being referenced by cryptographic commitments.

## Moodify as genesis, not boundary

Moodify is the first real protocol workload and the genesis application. Its original domain is sound and machine listening. In that domain, a task may request audio analysis, a model or agent may execute the task, the result may carry model version and evidence, a verifier may reproduce or challenge the output, and the resulting contribution may affect reputation or settlement. These mechanics are valuable because they exercise the general MOOD primitives under real conditions. They do not imply that the larger network is limited to music or sound.

# 4. MOOD as a State Transition System

## State abstraction

Following the state-transition framing used in early blockchain design, MOOD can be described abstractly as a system in which a valid action transforms one network state into another. This does not mean that every state component must live on one blockchain. It means that protocol behavior should be expressible as deterministic or auditable transitions over a known prior state plus an authorized action and its evidence references.

```text
APPLY_MOOD(S, a) -> S' or ERROR
```

Let the logical network state be represented as a tuple:

```text
S = (I, A, N, T, C, P, R, Q, G, E)
```

- I: identities and Passports, including key bindings and role claims.

- A: AI agents, capabilities, owners, delegations and revocation state.

- N: nodes and declared or verified resources.

- T: tasks, bounties, requests and execution conditions.

- C: contribution records and artifact references.

- P: proofs, evidence commitments and verification outcomes.

- R: reputation state, which may be multidimensional and domain-specific.

- Q: rights and permissions derived from identity, role, reputation, stake or governance.

- G: governance proposals, votes, approvals and executed protocol versions.

- E: economic state, including token balances, stakes, fees, rewards and Treasury commitments where applicable.

```text
STATE S
  │
  │ + ACTION a
  │   signed request + evidence references
  ▼
APPLY_MOOD(S, a)
  │
  ├── valid  -> STATE S'
  └── invalid -> ERROR

Validity depends on identity, authorization, protocol version,
evidence, and verification rules.
```

**Figure 2.** A valid action transforms network state only when protocol conditions are satisfied.

## Action classes

A minimal implementation need not support every possible action. The important classes are REGISTER_IDENTITY, BIND_KEY, REGISTER_AGENT, DELEGATE_AGENT, REGISTER_NODE, PUBLISH_TASK, CLAIM_TASK, SUBMIT_OUTPUT, COMMIT_EVIDENCE, VERIFY, RECORD_CONTRIBUTION, UPDATE_REPUTATION, SETTLE, PROPOSE, VOTE, EXECUTE_GOVERNANCE and REVOKE. Applications may define additional actions through versioned modules.

## Validity conditions

An action is valid only if its signature or authorization chain is valid; the actor exists or is being created under an allowed registration rule; the action is permitted by the actor's current rights; required evidence references are present; the target protocol module and version exist; anti-replay constraints such as nonce or unique action identifiers are satisfied; and any required verification, stake, payment or quorum conditions are met. Invalid actions must either be rejected or recorded only as non-state-changing observations, depending on the module.

The distinction between an observation and an accepted state transition is important. A participant may publish any claim about the world, but the network should not confuse publication with acceptance. Protocol modules define when a claim becomes a verified contribution, when a contribution affects reputation and when a verified result becomes eligible for settlement.

# 5. Identity and Passport

## Wallets are keys, not identities

A cryptographic wallet is an excellent authorization primitive and a poor complete identity model. People rotate keys, use multiple wallets, join multisignature accounts, operate agents and separate public from private activity. MOOD therefore distinguishes a key from a Passport. A Passport is a network identity object that can bind one or more keys and accumulate roles, contributions, reputation, badges, governance history and privacy preferences. A Passport may be anchored on-chain, represented off-chain with signed commitments, or use a hybrid method depending on the security requirements of the current version.

## Identity classes

MOOD recognizes several participant classes without assuming they require mutually exclusive namespaces. A Resident is a human-facing network identity. An Agent is a software actor operating under explicit authority. A Node is a resource provider or verification service with machine-readable status. An Application is an interface or protocol consumer. An Organization may be a multisignature entity, DAO, foundation, company, lab or informal collective. A single human may own several agents and participate in an organization while remaining one Resident.

## Passport fields

- Resident or actor identifier and creation time.

- Bound wallet keys, with optional labels, scopes and revocation history.

- Roles such as Developer, Creator, Researcher, Curator, Node Operator, Verifier, Agent Owner or Governor.

- Contribution references with source, task, time, evidence and verification state.

- Domain-specific reputation values and explanatory factors.

- Badges or attestations that are explicitly described as attestations rather than universal truth.

- Privacy controls specifying which data is public, private, local or shared only with authorized applications.

## Sybil resistance without identity absolutism

Some applications require one-person-one-vote properties; others do not. MOOD should not force a universal proof-of-personhood system onto every use case. Instead, protocol modules may specify the Sybil resistance mechanism appropriate to the decision: token stake, contribution history, reputation thresholds, verified organization membership, external identity attestations, social recovery, uniqueness providers or combinations of these. The mechanism must be visible to participants because the meaning of a vote depends on how membership was established.

# 6. Tasks, Contributions and Proof

## The task as a coordination primitive

A Task describes an intended unit of work that can be executed by a person, an agent, a node or a mixed group. The object may include a creator, scope, input references, required capabilities, deadlines, output schema, verification policy, privacy policy, budget or reward rule and dispute procedure. Tasks range from deterministic compute jobs to code contributions, research reviews, creative works and governance execution.

## Evidence before reward

A contribution should answer a simple set of questions: who or what performed the work, what was requested, what output was produced, when it occurred, what evidence exists, what protocol and software versions were used, who verified it, what the verification result was and what rights or settlement followed. MOOD calls the resulting record a Contribution Proof. The term proof does not imply zero-knowledge proof or mathematical certainty in every domain. It denotes an inspectable chain of evidence and validation under an explicit policy.

```text
TASK
  -> EXECUTION
  -> EVIDENCE
  -> VERIFICATION
  -> CONTRIBUTION RECORD
  -> REPUTATION / SETTLEMENT
```

**Figure 3.** The canonical task-to-contribution lifecycle. No reward should precede evidence, and evidence should not imply truth without verification.

## Contribution object

```text
C = H(actor_id || task_id || artifact_ref || evidence_root || timestamp || protocol_version)
```

The hash commitment is a compact identifier, not the contribution itself. Large artifacts may live in object storage, content-addressed networks, repositories or application databases. Sensitive artifacts may remain encrypted. The Contribution record contains the commitment plus metadata sufficient to locate or request authorized access to the underlying evidence.

## Verification models

Different tasks require different verification. Deterministic verification can rerun a computation and compare outputs. Statistical verification can compare metrics or confidence intervals. Peer verification can require independent reviewers. Reputation-weighted verification can use a set of specialized validators. Economic verification can require stake that is slashable for provably dishonest behavior. Social verification can record signed attestations without pretending they are objective. Governance verification can require approval under an MIP or committee process. A module may combine several methods.

## Disputes and finality

Contribution finality is not necessarily identical to blockchain finality. A payment transaction may be irreversible while a reputation judgment remains appealable. The protocol should therefore record verification status explicitly: submitted, provisionally verified, challenged, verified, rejected, superseded or revoked. Applications can choose which states are sufficient for access, display or settlement. This prevents a single binary flag from carrying more meaning than it can justify.

# 7. Reputation and Rights

## Reputation is not a transferable asset

Token balances can be transferred. Reputation should generally not be. MOOD treats reputation as an explanatory network state derived from history rather than a financial asset that can be bought directly. A participant may hold a large token balance and have little technical reputation; a researcher may have high domain reputation and almost no tokens. This separation reduces the tendency of financial wealth to collapse every other form of network standing into one dimension.

## Multidimensional reputation

There is no need for a universal MOOD score. Reputation may be a vector across domains such as software development, verification accuracy, research quality, node uptime, creative contribution, governance participation or agent reliability. Applications can interpret the vector differently. The protocol's obligation is to preserve provenance: which contributions influenced the value, under what policy and with what time weighting.

```text
R'_(actor,domain) = F(R_(actor,domain), verified_contribution, verifier_weight, time, disputes)
```

The function F is deliberately not fixed in this foundational paper. Fixing one equation would embed a social theory of merit before enough real network data exists. Each reputation module must nevertheless be deterministic or reproducible from public inputs whenever practical, versioned and explainable to the affected participant.

## Rights as outputs of state

Rights may be derived from several inputs: role, reputation, stake, contribution history, organizational membership, governance approval or explicit delegation. Examples include permission to verify certain tasks, eligibility for node work, access to a research dataset, ability to propose an MIP, participation in a grant round or increased rate limits. The rule that generates a right should be public even if the underlying private data is not.

# 8. AI Agents as First-Class Participants

## Agent identity

An AI Agent is a software actor with a persistent identifier, declared capabilities, execution environment references, owner or controller, permissions and revocation path. An agent may be stateless between tasks or maintain long-running memory. It may use one model or many. It may be fully autonomous within a narrow budget or require approval before each external action. MOOD does not define one agent architecture; it defines the coordination envelope in which agent actions can become attributable network actions.

## Delegation and authority

Agent authority should be explicit. A human or organization can delegate a scoped permission: for example, read a dataset, submit analyses, claim tasks below a budget threshold, operate a node, or vote only on a technical working-group proposal. High-risk privileges such as Treasury transfers, contract deployments, ownership changes and irreversible key operations should remain behind stronger controls, often including human signatures or multisignature policies. A compromised agent should not imply compromise of every asset associated with its owner.

## Execution records

For settlement-relevant work, an Agent Execution Record should include agent identity, task, software or model versions where available, tool invocations or summaries, output artifact, evidence commitment, resource usage, error status and signature or trusted execution attestation where applicable. Full chain-of-thought is not required and should not be treated as a security primitive. What matters is the externally inspectable record sufficient to reproduce or audit the result under the verification policy.

```text
             HUMANS
                │
                ▼
AI AGENTS -> PROTOCOL STATE <- APPLICATIONS
                ▲
                │
              NODES

Protocol state = shared rules + verifiable history
```

**Figure 4.** Humans, agents, nodes and applications interact through shared protocol state.

## Agent reputation

Agents can accumulate reputation independently from their owners. This allows an owner to operate multiple agents specialized for different tasks and makes reliability visible at the level where work is actually performed. The owner-agent link remains important for accountability and funding, but reputation should not be automatically inherited between the two. An agent may be forked, upgraded or replaced; version lineage should therefore be visible.

# 9. Nodes and Network Resources

## Node roles

A Node is a participant that provides measurable network service. Initial roles may include Compute Nodes that execute workloads, Storage Nodes that retain artifacts or data shards, Verification Nodes that independently check outputs, Indexing Nodes that make network state queryable, Relay Nodes that improve availability and domain-specific nodes introduced by future protocol modules. A single physical operator may provide several roles, but accounting should distinguish the service actually delivered.

## Proof of service

Node status must not be based only on purchasing a license or staking tokens. Stake can create economic accountability, but it does not prove that a server stored a file or executed a task. Node rewards therefore should reference service evidence: signed job receipts, challenge-response proofs, uptime observations, data availability proofs, reproducible compute outputs, verifier consensus or other domain-appropriate mechanisms. Where objective proof is not feasible, the network must label the assumption rather than disguise it.

## Resource markets

MOOD can support marketplaces in which tasks specify required resources and node operators advertise capacity and price. Matching can occur through centralized discovery services, decentralized order books, auctions or application-specific schedulers. Settlement can be direct between requester and provider or mediated by a protocol contract. The foundation layer should avoid prescribing a single market design because storage, compute and verification have different cost structures.

# 10. Protocol Modules

MOOD is intentionally modular. A monolithic protocol would make every upgrade politically and technically expensive and would force unrelated applications to share assumptions. A module defines a state subset, action types, validation rules, version identifier, upgrade policy and implementation references. Modules may depend on one another but should expose those dependencies explicitly.

## Proof System

The Proof System defines contribution records, evidence commitments, verifier identities, verification outcomes, dispute states and the mapping from verified work to reputation or settlement eligibility. It is the common spine connecting productive action to durable history.

## Agent Protocol

The Agent Protocol defines agent registration, controller relationships, capability declarations, scoped delegation, revocation, execution records and agent-specific reputation. It should support multiple agent frameworks and model providers rather than becoming a closed runtime.

## Node Protocol

The Node Protocol defines resource classes, registration, service evidence, status, penalties, discovery metadata and settlement interfaces. It explicitly rejects the idea that node membership alone constitutes contribution.

## Moodify Protocol

Moodify Protocol is the genesis vertical. It specifies machine-readable sound objects, analysis tasks, model or tool metadata, evidence, verification and domain-specific outputs. Its role is both practical and architectural: it gives the general network a real workload from which standards can evolve.

## Governance, Economic and Security Modules

Governance defines proposals and protocol upgrades. Economic modules define fees, stakes, rewards, Treasury flows and the use of MOOD. Security modules define key hierarchies, emergency pause powers, audit records, disclosure policy and the process for reducing privileged control over time. These modules are deliberately separated because economic incentives should not silently redefine identity, and emergency security powers should not silently become ordinary governance.

# 11. Economic Layer and MOOD

## Token is the value layer, not the world

MOOD is the native economic coordination asset of the network, but MOOD the token is not identical to MOOD the world. The world includes non-financial identity, contribution, reputation, culture, research and governance history. The token exists where a scarce transferable asset improves coordination. This separation is important because networks become brittle when every social interaction is forced into a speculative asset.

## Core functions

- Settlement: payment for protocol services, completed tasks, node work or other explicitly priced network activity.

- Incentive: rewards for verified contributions or public goods under defined programs.

- Staking: collateral for roles where economic accountability can reduce dishonest behavior.

- Governance input: one component of decision-making where economic exposure is relevant, without requiring every decision to be one-token-one-vote.

- Treasury accounting: a common asset for protocol development, grants, audits, infrastructure and ecosystem programs.

## Fees

A protocol fee should correspond to a real cost or economic function. Examples include settlement fees, verifier fees, storage or compute charges, application-level service fees and anti-spam deposits. Fees may be denominated in MOOD or in another asset where usability demands it, with conversion occurring at the application or settlement layer. Requiring every user interaction to hold MOOD in advance may create unnecessary friction; abstraction and sponsored transactions can be used where secure.

## Issuance and distribution

This foundational paper does not hard-code a supply curve, transaction tax, holder reward or allocation schedule. Those parameters are both economically consequential and implementation-specific. If a particular MOOD contract has a fixed supply, tax, reward mechanism or Treasury allocation, the canonical Token specification must publish the chain, contract, supply, admin powers, recipients and change process separately. The protocol thesis should remain intelligible even if an economic parameter is later revised through a legitimate governance process.

## Reputation versus capital

Some network rights may reasonably depend on stake; others should depend on contribution or expertise. A verifier of machine-listening research should not become trusted solely because of a large token balance. Conversely, a high-reputation participant should not be allowed to spend Treasury assets without the required economic and governance authorization. MOOD therefore treats capital, reputation and formal permission as separate state variables that can be combined by explicit rules.

# 12. Governance and Treasury

## MOOD Improvement Proposals

Protocol changes should be expressed through MOOD Improvement Proposals (MIPs). A proposal identifies the affected modules, motivation, technical specification, security considerations, migration plan, economic impact and rollback procedure. The canonical lifecycle is DRAFT -> DISCUSSION -> REVIEW -> VOTE -> ACCEPTED or REJECTED -> EXECUTED. Rejected proposals remain part of the public history because failed ideas are also evidence of network reasoning.

## Progressive governance

Early-stage networks often need a smaller group to respond quickly to bugs, legal obligations and infrastructure failures. Pretending that no privileged control exists is worse than documenting it. MOOD therefore supports progressive governance: privileged keys and committees may exist, but their powers, members, thresholds, expiration or review rules should be public. The roadmap should reduce single points of control as the protocol, monitoring and contributor base mature.

## Treasury

The Treasury is a public resource pool, not a promise of yield. Its addresses, major assets and categorized flows should be visible. Expenditure classes may include protocol development, audits, infrastructure, research, grants, ecosystem incentives and operations. Material Treasury decisions should link to an MIP, multisignature action or other verifiable authorization record. AI Agents may prepare proposals or execute low-risk administrative steps, but irreversible movement of high-value assets should remain under explicit key and approval policies.

# 13. Chain Architecture and Data Availability

## Protocol-first, chain-agnostic

MOOD does not require an independent Layer 1 blockchain at genesis. Building a new consensus network imposes large costs in client software, validator bootstrapping, networking, security monitoring, wallets, bridges and liquidity. These costs are justified only if the coordination model eventually requires execution semantics or throughput that existing networks cannot provide. Until then, existing smart-contract chains can provide cryptographic settlement, stakes, token transfers, governance commitments and durable state roots.

```text
RICH OFF-CHAIN STATE
profiles · artifacts · execution logs · large evidence · private / permissioned data
            │
            │ commit / anchor
            ▼
ON-CHAIN COMMITMENTS
identifiers · signatures · hashes / roots · settlement · stakes · governance
            ▲
            │ verify / settle
            └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MOOD is protocol-first and chain-agnostic.
An independent L1 is not a prerequisite.
```

**Figure 5.** Large artifacts remain off-chain while compact commitments and economic state can be anchored on-chain.

## Hybrid state

The recommended architecture separates rich operational data from compact commitments. Profiles, large media, model outputs, source repositories, private documents and execution traces may live off-chain. The chain stores identifiers, signatures, hashes, roots, stakes, settlement events and governance decisions. An application can verify that an artifact corresponds to a recorded commitment without paying the cost of storing the artifact itself on every consensus node.

## Content addressing and availability

A hash proves integrity only if the underlying content remains available to an authorized verifier. Applications should therefore record both integrity commitments and availability locations or retrieval policies. Public artifacts may be replicated through content-addressed storage; private artifacts may be encrypted and stored with access controls; critical governance or audit documents may use multiple independent mirrors. The network should not equate 'hash on chain' with durable storage.

## Anchoring network state

Off-chain services may periodically commit Merkle roots or other aggregate hashes of Passport, contribution or execution datasets. A verifier can then request a proof that a record belonged to a particular committed state. This allows applications to provide high-throughput user experiences while retaining an auditable link to public commitments. The exact tree format and anchoring frequency are implementation decisions and may evolve by module.

# 14. Security and Adversarial Model

## Threat classes

- Key compromise: theft or misuse of human, agent, node, multisignature or administrative keys.

- Sybil attacks: one operator creates many identities, agents or nodes to dominate a voting or reward mechanism.

- False evidence: a participant submits fabricated, incomplete or misleading artifacts.

- Verifier collusion: validators coordinate to approve invalid work or reject honest work.

- Agent compromise: malicious prompts, tools, dependencies or model behavior cause an agent to exceed intended authority.

- Node fraud: providers claim service they did not actually deliver or manipulate resource measurements.

- Governance capture: concentrated wealth, apathy, bribery or rushed procedures produce harmful protocol changes.

- Data availability failure: a commitment remains verifiable in theory while the referenced content disappears.

- Spam and griefing: cheap actions impose verification or storage costs on other participants.

- Implementation risk: smart contracts, bridges, indexers, APIs, front ends and off-chain databases contain defects.

## Security principles

The security model follows least privilege. Agent keys should not hold unnecessary Treasury authority. Contract deployment and upgrade keys should be isolated from ordinary application operations. Critical changes should use multisignature or equivalent threshold controls. Public interfaces should display chain IDs, contract versions and admin powers. Versioned protocol documents should map to actual implementation references. Security incidents and emergency actions should be recorded as part of network history rather than hidden as operational details.

## Economic security is not sufficient

Staking can deter behavior only when misconduct is detectable and attributable. A large stake does not make a subjective answer true, and slashing rules can themselves be exploited if verification is weak. MOOD therefore uses economic penalties only in domains where evidence and dispute procedures justify them. Other domains may rely more heavily on reputation, peer review, access control or social governance.

## Privacy

Open participation does not imply total public disclosure. Personal profiles, private task inputs, proprietary models and regulated data may require confidentiality. The protocol should support commitments to private evidence and selective disclosure rather than forcing plaintext publication. Privacy mechanisms may include encryption, access-control lists, zero-knowledge proofs, trusted execution or application-specific legal controls. The important requirement is that a verifier understand what assumptions protect the claim.

# 15. Scalability and Modularity

## Scale the expensive thing last

MOOD should not make global consensus perform work that can be verified locally. The majority of network actions - reading a profile, viewing a world map, browsing contributions, running an AI model or storing a large file - do not require consensus on every byte. The globally expensive layer should be reserved for commitments, economic transfers, governance outcomes and disputes whose integrity benefits from shared finality.

## Domain-specific verification

Verification scales when work is partitioned by domain. Sound analysis, software tests, storage proofs, research peer review and governance votes have different validators and data needs. Modular verification sets allow specialized participants to handle work they understand. Cross-domain applications can compose the resulting proofs without requiring every network participant to reproduce every task.

## Indexing and light clients

A practical network interface will rely on indexers for query performance. Indexers are not necessarily trusted authorities if critical records can be checked against signatures and anchored commitments. Client software can use a light verification mode: fetch a Passport or contribution record from an indexer, validate the actor signature, validate the inclusion proof against a known root and optionally retrieve the underlying evidence. Full archival nodes can support deeper auditing.

## Future appchain or rollup

If network activity becomes large enough that fees, latency or custom verification semantics become a bottleneck, MOOD may adopt a dedicated rollup, appchain, validity system or other execution environment. Such a migration should be justified by measured demand. Creating an independent chain before the coordination primitives have real usage would optimize the wrong layer.

# 16. WORLD and PORTAL as the Network Interface

## WORLD: a place with memory

WORLD is not a technical dependency of cryptographic verification, but it is a social dependency of a durable digital community. It gives the network a visual language, manifesto, public spaces and navigational geography. Library, Protocol Hall, Builder Workshop, Agent Lab, Node Station and Moodify Gate are not merely menu labels; they are a spatial grammar for understanding the network. A participant should be able to enter MOOD without first reading a token chart.

## PORTAL: from visitor to resident

PORTAL turns network concepts into actions. The canonical early path is Visitor -> Connect Wallet -> Resident -> Contributor -> Reputation -> Governance / Rights / Rewards. The order matters. Connecting a wallet is the beginning, not the achievement. A blank dashboard with a token balance does not constitute participation. The first successful Portal should make at least one contribution traceable from task to proof to history.

## Network interface, not project website

crestwavecoin.com is intended to become the canonical MOOD Network Interface: a place to read rules, inspect network state, enter through a wallet or Passport, see real agents and nodes, examine MIPs and Treasury records, discover applications and contribute. The site should display real counts and explicit data definitions. If there is one node, it should show one node. An honest network state is more valuable than a fabricated global scale.

# 17. Genesis Application: Moodify

## Why sound

A general coordination protocol needs a concrete domain in which its abstractions encounter friction. Moodify provides that domain. Sound analysis is computational, creative and partially subjective. It involves large artifacts, machine models, measurable audio properties, interpretation, versioned tooling and potential human review. This makes it a useful test of identity, task execution, evidence, reproducibility, domain reputation and resource provisioning.

## Example lifecycle

A creator or application submits an audio-analysis task. The task references an audio object and specifies a policy. An authorized Agent or Node retrieves the artifact, runs a declared model or toolchain and submits an output plus an evidence commitment. One or more verifiers rerun deterministic components or inspect domain-specific claims. The network records the accepted Contribution Proof. The agent, developer, model maintainer, verifier or compute provider may gain domain reputation or receive settlement according to the module. The result can then be consumed by another application without that application needing to trust the original front end.

## The boundary principle

```text
MOOD
open digital world / coordination network
        │
        ▼
MOODIFY PROTOCOL
sound + AI + proof as the genesis vertical
        │
        ▼
MOODIFY
genesis application / first real workload
        │
        ▼
FUTURE PROTOCOLS & APPLICATIONS
research · compute · creativity · software · public goods · other domains
```

**Figure 6.** Moodify is the first protocol/application pair; future domains reuse the same coordination primitives.

> **Sound is the genesis of MOOD, not the boundary of MOOD.**

The architectural rule is simple: Sound is the genesis of MOOD, not the boundary of MOOD. The protocol must not hard-code music-specific semantics into the root identity, contribution, governance or settlement layers. Domain semantics belong in Moodify Protocol. The general MOOD network remains available to future protocols whose artifacts are not sound at all.

# 18. Application Classes

## Open software development

Repositories can publish tasks, contributors can bind commits or pull requests to Passports, reviewers can verify deliverables and contribution history can become portable across projects. Grants or bounties can settle only after defined evidence is accepted. The network does not replace Git; it provides a coordination and reputation layer across repositories and organizations.

## Research networks

Researchers can register datasets, analyses, reproductions, reviews and negative results. Agents can perform literature scans or experiment runs under recorded versions. Reputation can be domain-specific and tied to reproducibility rather than popularity. Grants can reference milestones and evidence. Sensitive data can remain permissioned while commitments remain public.

## AI labor and agent services

Users can delegate scoped tasks to agents and discover agents through capability and reliability history. Agent owners can compete on verified performance rather than only marketing claims. Applications can require a minimum reputation or stake for certain workloads. Disputes can reference execution evidence and version lineage.

## Creative production

Creators can coordinate contributors, tools, models and rights references across a production pipeline. MOOD does not attempt to decide aesthetic truth. It records who contributed what, what tools were used, what was verified and what settlement or attribution followed. Moodify is the first example, but the same structure can extend to visual, interactive or mixed-media workflows.

## Network resource markets

Compute, storage, verification and indexing services can become composable resource markets. A protocol can request resources, nodes can supply them and service evidence can determine settlement. Applications remain free to use cloud providers or centralized infrastructure; the network resource layer becomes valuable where openness, redundancy or independent verification matters.

## Public goods and communities

Communities can maintain transparent Treasury programs, contribution registries and governance histories. A grant does not need to become a corporation employment relationship. Contributors can build durable standing across several public-good projects while each project retains its own verification and funding rules.

# 19. Roadmap and Network Metrics

## Phase 0 - Canon and scope

Freeze the hierarchy between MOOD, protocol modules, Moodify and MOOD Token. Maintain one canonical public rule set. Remove duplicate concepts and prevent implementation work from silently expanding the scope.

## Phase 1 - Network Interface

Converge WORLD, PROTOCOL, LIBRARY, NETWORK and PORTAL on crestwavecoin.com with real data sources. Publish versioned documents, implementation references and a network status surface.

## Phase 2 - Passport and Contribution

Launch the minimum resident loop: wallet connection, Passport creation, task or contribution submission, evidence, verification and reputation history. This is the first phase in which MOOD becomes participatory rather than descriptive.

## Phase 3 - Agents and Nodes

Register real agents and nodes performing real tasks. Expose capabilities, execution or service evidence, verification state and contribution history. Avoid multiplying empty agent categories or node types for presentation.

## Phase 4 - Governance and Treasury

Open MIP history, Treasury transparency, role permissions and protocol upgrade workflows. Reduce single-party controls where security and participation allow.

## Phase 5 - Open ecosystem

Enable third parties to build applications, agents, tools and protocol modules that use MOOD identity, proof, reputation and settlement primitives without requiring ownership by the original Moodify team.

## Metrics

Network health should be measured by reality rather than feature count or market price. Canonical metrics include Residents, Token Holders, Developers, Creators, AI Agents, Nodes, Contributions, Applications, MIPs and Treasury state. Each metric should publish its definition, source and snapshot time. A real one is more valuable than an invented ten thousand.

# 20. Open Questions

MOOD is deliberately incomplete where premature certainty would be harmful. Several questions require experiments and governance rather than whitepaper decree.

- What is the minimum Passport data required for portability without creating unnecessary privacy risk?

- Which contribution classes can be objectively verified and which should remain explicitly social or subjective?

- How should reputation decay, delegation and recovery work across long time horizons?

- Which actions justify economic staking or slashing, and which should rely on non-financial accountability?

- How should Agent owners disclose model or tool dependencies while protecting legitimate proprietary information?

- What minimum service proofs make Compute, Storage and Verification Nodes economically credible?

- How should token voting, contribution reputation and one-person or one-entity identity interact in different governance domains?

- Which network state deserves on-chain finality, and which is better served by signed off-chain records plus periodic commitments?

- At what scale would a dedicated rollup or appchain improve the system enough to justify migration risk?

- How should protocol modules interoperate while preserving independent upgrade paths and security boundaries?

The network should treat these questions as research areas with public experiments, measurements and MIPs. The purpose of a foundational protocol is not to eliminate uncertainty. It is to make the process of changing assumptions visible and governable.

# 21. Conclusion

MOOD proposes a network architecture for a world in which humans and AI systems increasingly create together but do not necessarily belong to the same company, platform or jurisdiction. The core abstraction is open coordination state: durable identities, delegated agents, measurable resources, tasks, evidence, verification, contribution history, reputation, rights, governance and settlement connected by versioned public rules.

The design intentionally resists two reductions. First, MOOD is not reduced to a token. Economic assets are useful when they coordinate scarce resources, but identity, reputation, culture and public history must remain intelligible without a price chart. Second, MOOD is not reduced to its first application. Moodify and sound intelligence provide the genesis workload because real protocols need real work. The general network is designed to support many future domains.

The near-term objective is therefore modest in implementation but large in direction: make the network enterable, inspectable, participatory and verifiable. One Passport with a real contribution, one agent with a real execution record, one node with real service evidence and one governance action with a public trail are more important than an elaborate simulation of a mature ecosystem.

Bitcoin demonstrated that public consensus could secure monetary history. Ethereum demonstrated that programmable state could become a general platform. MOOD explores the next coordination question: can an open network give people, machines and resources a shared place to act, prove, build and leave history without requiring a single platform to own the relationship? The answer will not come from the whitepaper alone. It will come from whether the network can make those primitives real.

## Implementation Boundary for Coding Agents

This document defines **architecture, protocol intent, terminology, and boundaries**. It does not by itself prove that a feature exists in the repository or is deployed on a live network.

Before changing code, a coding agent should:

1. Identify the relevant MOOD layer or protocol module.
2. Check the repository's current canonical implementation files and versioned configuration.
3. Preserve the hierarchy `MOOD > protocol modules > applications`.
4. Keep Moodify-specific sound semantics out of root MOOD identity, contribution, governance, and settlement primitives.
5. Require evidence before marking contribution as verified or settlement-eligible.
6. Treat reputation and transferable token balances as separate state dimensions.
7. Use explicit delegation and revocation for AI Agent authority.
8. Treat node membership or token stake as insufficient proof of real service by itself.
9. Prefer hybrid on-chain/off-chain commitments when full on-chain storage is unnecessary.
10. Do not invent live metrics, addresses, governance state, issuance parameters, or deployed capabilities.
